tasks.short: Walk the workshop and sites for hazards, inspect tools and lifting gear, record findings, correct behaviour and give safety talks.

steps.what: Supervisor walks the workshop and job sites looking for unsafe conditions
Supervisor examines tools, lifting gear and ladders and works out which are due for inspection
Supervisor writes findings: on a paper checklist typed into a spreadsheet today, once on a phone checklist after the change
Supervisor checks the actions raised from the findings: what is wrong, where, the owner and the due date
Supervisor releases the checked actions to their owners in the maintenance management system
Supervisor corrects unsafe work and violations of procedures on the spot
Supervisor gives toolbox talks and safety training to the team
Mechanics sign attendance for the safety talk on the tablet
Supervisor keeps attendance lists of safety talks: on paper today; after the change the supervisor checks the signed list in the {LMS}
Safety advisor reviews findings and trends

tasks.design: Tools and lifting gear carry a tag and an inspection due date in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}), which lists what is due each week. The supervisor writes findings once on a phone checklist instead of on paper and again in a spreadsheet, checks the actions raised with their owners and due dates, and releases them once to the owners' work lists. Mechanics sign attendance at toolbox talks on a tablet into the {LMS}; walking, judging and teaching stay with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Inspection dates, findings and attendance lived on paper and in spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems hold asset registers with due dates and mobile checklists; learning systems take sign-ins on tablets.
tasks.still_hard: Spotting hazards is judgement; recording violations per person needs works council consent.
tasks.human_edge: Stopping a job that looks wrong and making safety a habit, not a form.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; less paperwork after each round.

reach.learn: Whether photo checklists give better trend data.

evidence.claim: Maintenance systems keep asset registers with inspection due dates and mobile checklists.
Rules on staff data and systems able to monitor behaviour need works council consent.
Employers must inform and instruct workers about safety risks under national working conditions rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from inspection rounds to findings and training recorded; investigating accidents is outside.
Input contract: tool register with tag numbers and inspection intervals kept by the supervisor and the safety advisor; checklist items set by the safety advisor; fallback is paper.
Findings are recorded per location and tool, not per worker.

Safety advisor time is outside the supervisor's savings. Walking, correcting, teaching, the action check and the release keep their full time. s2 keeps 70 because the due list replaces working out which tools are due; s3 keeps 55 because typing goes and writing the findings stays; s6 keeps 20 for checking the signed list. The mechanics' sign-in is step s5b (share 1).
unknowns: Number of tools and lifting gear items in the register.
How often toolbox talks are held.
research_questions: Do photo findings close faster than paper findings?

incremental.description: Supervisor tags and registers new tools.
Safety advisor keeps checklist items and inspection intervals current.

approvals.approved_version: The actions with finding, location, owner and due date exactly as checked by the supervisor in s3b, released once to the named owners' work lists in the maintenance management system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the tool register is not kept current, so the supervisor still works out what is due (7.1); high: the due list is current (12.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Get the current drawings and job order, interpret them, measure and mark reference points, build templates and brief the mechanics.

steps.what: Supervisor fetches the latest drawing revision and specifications from the office
Supervisor interprets the specifications, blueprints and job order
Supervisor measures on site and lays out reference points
Supervisor constructs templates and jigs for the workers
Supervisor explains the layout and templates to the mechanics
Supervisor writes up deviations from the drawing: on paper today, as a mark-up on the tablet drawing with the job order number after the change
Supervisor checks the marked-up deviations: what differs, where on the drawing, the revision and the job order
Supervisor sends the checked mark-up to engineering

tasks.design: Job orders in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}) link to the current drawing revision in {DOCS}, opened on a tablet on site, so the supervisor no longer fetches paper copies. The supervisor marks deviations up on the tablet drawing with the job order number, checks the mark-up and sends it once to engineering; interpretation, layout and template work stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Drawings were paper copies, and revisions reached the floor late.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems link documents to job orders and run on tablets.
tasks.still_hard: Laying out reference points and building templates are hands-on skills.
tasks.human_edge: Reading a drawing against the real installation and seeing where it will not fit.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; the right revision is always at hand.

reach.learn: Whether tablet mark-ups keep drawings current.

evidence.claim: Maintenance systems link drawings and documents to job orders and run on tablets.
An enterprise asset management system offers ERP and supply-chain links and downtime reporting by technicians.

assumptions: Boundary: from receiving the job order to the mechanics briefed and deviations reported; the work itself is outside.
Input contract: drawings with revision numbers kept by engineering in the document store and linked to assets; fallback is paper copies.
Engineering time is outside the supervisor's savings.

Interpretation, layout, templates, the mark-up check and the send keep their full time. s1 keeps 30 for opening and checking the revision on the tablet; s6 keeps 85 because the deviations are still written, and only finding the drawing and job references goes.
unknowns: Whether drawings are digital and linked to assets.
How many layout jobs per month.
research_questions: Do rework cases from outdated drawings fall?

incremental.description: Supervisor keeps the tablet synced and reports missing links.
Engineering links drawing revisions to assets and job orders.

approvals.approved_version: The marked-up drawing with the deviations, drawing revision and job order number exactly as checked by the supervisor in s6c, sent once to engineering's queue for that drawing; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the site has no reliable tablet access, so paper copies and paper write-ups stay (-0.3); high: drawings linked and opened on the tablet (7.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Track who is on which job, compare hours with estimates per job, check finished work, coach mechanics and prepare reviews.

steps.what: Mechanics update job status and book actual hours on job orders on their phones
Supervisor goes round to see who is on which job and how far along it is
Supervisor compares work levels and hours booked with job estimates in a spreadsheet
Supervisor checks the quality of finished work on site
Supervisor gives feedback and coaching to mechanics
Supervisor prepares annual performance reviews of employees from loose notes
Supervisor holds the review conversations

tasks.design: Mechanics update job status on their phones in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}), giving a team board of open, running and waiting jobs, and a report per job order shows hours against estimate. Coaching notes are kept through the year in the {TALENT} system; no view ranks or scores individual mechanics, and judgement stays with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Job status was known only by walking round, and hours against estimates were rebuilt in spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems take job updates from phones and report hours per job order.
tasks.still_hard: Hours per mechanic are performance data; the works council must agree, and AI that evaluates workers would be high-risk.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing who is struggling or stretched and helping them grow.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; status is visible without a round.

reach.learn: Whether hours per job order improve estimates.

evidence.claim: An enterprise asset management system lets technicians report downtime and work from the floor.
Systems able to monitor attendance, behaviour or performance, and time records per mechanic, need works council consent.
AI that monitors and evaluates workers' performance is high-risk from 2 December 2027.

assumptions: Boundary: from tracking daily work to review conversations; pay and promotion are outside.
Input contract: job status and hours booked by mechanics on job orders; estimates set by the maintenance planner; fallback is walking round and spreadsheets.
Reports are per job order and team; individual data is used only in the supervisor's own conversations, as agreed with the works council.

Mechanics' time on status and hours updates is step s0 (share 1, other role). s1 keeps 70 because the supervisor still goes round to see the work; s2 keeps 40 for reading the overrun report; s5 keeps 70 because notes are in one place and the supervisor still writes each review.
unknowns: Whether mechanics book hours on job orders today.
research_questions: Does a live job board reduce waiting time between jobs?

already_counted.description: Supervisor reviews the overrun list per job order.

incremental.description: Supervisor reminds mechanics to update job status.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mechanics update status on only about half of jobs, so most rounds stay (16.2); high: status kept current on the board (19.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check parts stock, requisition parts, track lent tools, inspect workshop conditions and raise repair requests for the shop.

steps.what: Mechanics book parts out on job orders and scan the tools they borrow
Supervisor checks part inventories on the shelves for items running low
Supervisor reviews reorder lines: e-mails parts requests today; after the change the system proposes reorders from minimum levels and the supervisor adjusts them
Supervisor checks the final reorder lines: parts, quantities, the job orders they serve and that each need is real
Supervisor releases the checked reorder lines to the procurement system
Buyer checks the order: parts, quantities, supplier and delivery address
Buyer orders the parts from suppliers
Supervisor tracks tools lent out: on a paper list today; after the change the supervisor checks the list built from mechanics' scans
Supervisor inspects the condition of shops: lighting, ventilation, housekeeping, machines
Supervisor writes requests for shop repairs: by phone to facilities today, in the maintenance management system after the change
Supervisor checks the final repair request: the shop issue, location and urgency
Supervisor submits the checked repair request to facilities
Facilities technician repairs the shop issue

tasks.design: Parts get minimum and maximum levels in the maintenance management system ({OTHER}); mechanics book parts out on job orders, the system proposes reorders, and the supervisor adjusts them, checks the final lines and releases them once to the {PROCUREMENT} system, where the buyer checks and places the order. Mechanics scan tools they borrow, so the supervisor checks the loan list instead of keeping it. The supervisor writes shop repair requests in the same system, checks each and submits it once; inspecting the shop stays with the supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stock lived on shelves and in heads, with maintenance partly followed up in spreadsheets.
tasks.enabler_now: Maintenance systems link parts stock, job orders and purchasing; a documented case moved from spreadsheets to such a system with large drops in breakdown time.
tasks.still_hard: Stock is only right if mechanics book every part out; urgent parts still go by phone.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which spare part will stop the plant if it is missing.

ambition.what: Critical spares checked against levels every day instead of when someone notices an empty shelf.

tasks.altitude: The supervisor confirms reorders instead of counting; buying stays with purchasing.

reach.task: Issue parts and keep stock records
reach.learn: Whether booking on job orders lowers stock differences.

evidence.claim: An enterprise asset management system links maintenance with ERP and supply chain.

A Belgian lubricants plant that had followed maintenance partly in spreadsheets cut breakdown time from about 300 to 115 hours a month and saved about EUR 360,000 a year after moving to such a system (vendor case).
A food maker with 12 sites reported about 30% less downtime after moving to preventive work (vendor case, no baseline).

assumptions: Boundary: from checking stock and shop to reorders placed and repairs requested; supplier selection is outside.
Input contract: min/max levels per part set by the supervisor with the planner; parts booked out by mechanics on job orders; tools tagged for scanning; fallback is shelf checks and e-mail.
Buyer, mechanic and facilities time is outside the supervisor's savings. The mechanics' booking and scanning is step s0 (share 1, other role).

Shop inspection, writing repair requests, the checks and the releases keep their full time. s1 keeps 40 for spot checks of the shelves; s2 keeps 40 for adjusting proposals; s4 keeps 30 for checking the loan list.
unknowns: Whether parts are booked on job orders today.
research_questions: Do stock-outs of critical spares fall after min/max levels?

already_counted.description: Supervisor reviews and confirms reorder proposals.

incremental.description: Supervisor runs short cycle counts to correct stock.

approvals.approved_version: The reorder lines with part, quantity and job order exactly as checked by the supervisor in s2c, released once to the {PROCUREMENT} system for the buyer; any change needs a new check.
The purchase order with parts, quantities, supplier and delivery address exactly as checked by the buyer in s3c, sent once to the named supplier; any change needs a new check.

The repair request with shop issue, location and urgency exactly as checked by the supervisor in s6c, submitted once to the facilities queue in the maintenance management system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mechanics do not book parts out reliably, so shelf checks and hand-made requests largely return (17.1); high: parts booked out on job orders (31.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The maintenance supervisor keeps rounds, judgement and coaching; tool registers, stock and job status move into the maintenance system.
skills_to_grow: Running the maintenance system's lists and reorders
Using job data without ranking people
role.ambitious_version: A supervisor who sees every job, part and due inspection on one screen and spends the day on the floor.

job.title: First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics, Installers, and Repairers
